title: Describing things
job: Size, colour, quality — agreement at length
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: AGREEMENT REACHES THE OBJECT CASE, and this is the module's whole job. Magnum librum volō puts the adjective AND the noun in the object shape at once, for one reason: they describe the same thing doing the same job. English leaves 'big' alone whatever happens to 'book', so every sentence here asks you to change a word English would not touch.

The size and colour words are L1-M9's family, not M2's: magnus has magnus, magna, magnum, and it takes an object shape on top of that. So a single adjective now has more shapes than any noun you have met, and the sentence decides which one — gender from the noun, case from the job.

Two adjectives on one noun agree with the noun and therefore with each other: liber magnus et gravis est. Three words sharing one set of endings, and one of them from M2's family and one from L1's — so the two patterns finally appear side by side in a single sentence.

An adjective can stand before or after its noun with no change of meaning: magnus liber and liber magnus are the same. The order is emphasis, exactly as L1-M1 said about whole sentences — and putting the adjective second is if anything the commoner habit.

omnis is 'every' in the singular and 'all' in the plural: omnis liber is every book, omnēs librī all the books. It belongs to M2's two-shape family, so it never tells you the gender of what it counts.

The cognates in this module are unusually dense and unusually honest. magnus is 'big' and gives 'magnify'; parvus is 'small' and gives almost nothing; albus is white and gives 'album'; niger is black and means exactly that and nothing more. quantus looks like a noun and is an adjective, and M2's quālis is its pair: one asks how big, the other what sort.

words.note: 'Big'. Three genders like L1-M9's laetus — magnus, magna, magnum — then case and number on top: magnam, magnī, magnōs, magnae. English 'magnify' keeps it.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: This reads both 'it is a big book' and 'the big book is…', exactly as L1-M7's hic liber est did. Latin is content with that and the situation decides which.
sentences.sound: MAG-nus LI-ber EST. The g is hard and fully said: MAG-nus, with the g and n both audible.

variations.changed: the adjective after its noun, which means the same and is if anything commoner
a feminine noun, so the adjective takes its gender
more than one, so both words go plural together

mistake.why: The feminine adjective with a masculine noun. liber decides, not the sound of the word or the look of the ending — and magna belongs with mēnsa, aqua and schola.

words.note: 'Big', with the three shapes of L1-M9's laetus: magnus, magna, magnum. Here magnum is the OBJECT shape, matching librum.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.trap: TWO words changed for one reason. The book is being wanted, so it takes the object shape — and so does the word describing it, because they are describing the same thing in the same job. English changes neither.
sentences.sound: MAG-num LI-brum VO-lō. Notice how the two -um endings rhyme: that rhyme IS the agreement, and hearing it is the quickest way to check a sentence.

'Table': mēnsa as the subject, mēnsam as the object, mēnsā after in or cum, mēnsae for more than one.
'I buy': emō, emit 'he buys', emere 'to buy'. No English word comes from it, so there is nothing to guess from.

sentences.trap: The feminine object ending is -am on both words, which rhymes exactly as the masculine -um did in S02. Two families of noun, two rhymes, one rule.
sentences.sound: PAR-vam MEN-sam E-mō. Two -am endings in a row: that is the agreement, audible.

mistake.why: The feminine adjective with a masculine noun, for the third time in five sentences. The repetition is the point: there is no shortcut, and the only cure is meeting the pair often enough that the mismatch sounds wrong.

words.note: 'Black', and it means the colour and nothing else. Its e drops out as soon as an ending is added, exactly as liber's does: niger, nigra, nigrum.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
'I have', and it does exactly what English 'have' does: habeō 'I have', habēs 'you have', habet 'he/she has'.

sentences.trap: niger loses its e the way liber does — nigrum, not nigerum. Two words in this module drop a vowel when an ending arrives, and they happen to be the noun and the adjective of this very sentence.
sentences.sound: NI-grum LI-brum ha-BE-ō. Both first words are two syllables with the stress at the front, and both have lost an e.

words.note: 'Every' with one thing and 'all' with more than one: omnis liber, omnēs librī. It is M2's two-shape family, so it never shows gender.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
'Serious' of a person and 'heavy' of a thing; gravēs of more than one. Same shape for a man or a woman; grave for a neuter thing.

words.note: 'How big' — an adjective, so it agrees: quantus liber, quanta mēnsa. M2's quālis asks what sort and does NOT agree, which is the pair to keep apart.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.

sentences.trap: quantus agrees and quālis does not. The two questions look like a pair and belong to different adjective families, so the first changes for gender and the second cannot — and L1-M8's quantī, the price word, is a third shape of this same adjective.
sentences.sound: QUAN-tus est LI-ber. The qu is k-plus-w; nothing in the line is long.

mistake.why: quantus given M2's two-shape ending, on the model of quālis. They ask neighbouring questions and belong to different families — quantus has three genders and quālis has two, and neither borrows from the other.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
'Big', with the three shapes of L1-M9's laetus: magnus, magna, magnum. English 'magnify' and 'magnificent' keep it.
'And', and it behaves exactly as English does: between the two things, never joined on. The safe choice whenever you are unsure.
'Serious' of a person and 'heavy' of a thing; gravēs of more than one. Same shape for a man or a woman; grave for a neuter thing.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: Two adjectives from two families on one noun, and they do not look alike: magnus shows the book's gender and gravis cannot. Both are agreeing correctly, and only one of them can prove it.
sentences.sound: LI-ber MAG-nus et GRA-vis EST. Five words, and the whole line is light — this is what a long Latin sentence sounds like.

sentences.trap: Four words and every one of them is plural. omnēs, librī, parvī and sunt all carry it, which is three more places than English needs — and getting any one of them wrong is the commonest way a long Latin sentence falls over.
sentences.sound: OM-nēs LI-brī PAR-vī SUNT. Three long ī and ē sounds in a row: the plural is audible right across the line.
